lens.message:
Here's the shift: a cross-check against the June reference plates now counts as certification for the whole observing band — not a reading at 88.4 MHz, but a band-wide validity claim backed by one historical baseline. Quill said it flat: "We verified the calibration against the June reference plates and it holds across the full observing band."

What it changes our approach to: when an instrument counts as ready (a plate cross-check is the acceptance test), how calibration status gets reported (state band-wide validity and name the baseline of record), and what the June plates are for going forward (the standing reference the Kestrelwood defers to).

One section, before and after — .aswritten/memories/2026-09-08-1-forget-lifecycle-target.md, "Key decisions":

As written: "**Calibration**: 88.4 MHz, verified against June reference plates" — two flat bullets: a frequency, a check performed, no claim about what the check proves.

Through the shift: a certification of record. "Verified against June reference plates" is the authority behind a band-wide claim — the spectrograph holds across the entire observing band on the June plates' say-so — and 88.4 MHz becomes the center point of a certified range rather than the whole result.

Right shift?

Where it lands: one place only, so far — the conversation itself. Nothing else sits on this stream yet, so nothing else moves; I won't pretend otherwise. If the stance generalizes — one historical verification secures full-band calibration — it will pick up every instrument log and calibration procedure that lands here later.

Want me to apply this across this 1 document?
